name: Boa
lede: Boa is a soft yellow-green that Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates to 1892, close enough to the library's Asphodel Green and Sage that only a few measured units tell them apart.

sections.title: A 1892 name, origin unexplained
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's *A Dictionary of Color* (1930) places Boa on plate 19, position B5, and dates its first recorded use to 1892 [1]. The dictionary does not explain why the word *boa*, which also names a feathered scarf and the snake, was attached to this shade of green, so its origin is undocumented here [1]. The ISCC-NBS 1955 lists do not carry the name separately; the National Bureau of Standards circular cites only Maerz and Paul's entry [1].

The library's measurements put this swatch closest to [[asphodel-green|Asphodel Green]], 3.0 units off, and within about 3.7 units of [[sage|Sage]], a cooler, greyer green that is one of the more common names in everyday use [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a color match to this swatch in 193 of 23,781 paintings, 0.81 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 110, more common than 60 percent of the named colors we track [3]. Pierre-Auguste Renoir is its most devoted painter, carrying it in 4 of the 50 [[painter:auguste-renoir|Renoir]] paintings in the archive, 5.1 times the rate expected from the museums his works come from [3].

The color peaks in the 1910s, 2.5 times the expected rate across 523 paintings from that decade, and inside a painting it most often sits as a light tone (40 percent of its 110 within-painting matches) [3]. The earliest match dates to 1420, nearly five centuries before the name's 1892 record, which shows only that a similar-looking hue existed in paint long before the word did, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. India is the most over-represented country, at 2.7 times its expected share, and the Rajput and Impressionist schools both carry it well above the archive's average [3]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, read as screen colors [3].
